title: Web & wireless security
learningGoals: You will be able to diagram the 1-RTT TLS 1.3 cryptographic handshake.
You will be able to explain how HTTPS protects web traffic against tampering and eavesdropping.
You will be able to describe the WPA3 Dragonfly (SAE) handshake protecting Wi-Fi.

lessonCards.title: The 1-RTT TLS 1.3 Handshake
lessonCards.analogy: A lightning-fast secret introduction: client and server agree on keys in just one round-trip exchange.
lessonCards.coreConcept: TLS 1.3 replaced slow legacy protocols: 1. ClientHello sends supported ciphers and Diffie-Hellman key share. 2. ServerHello replies with its key share and digital certificate. 3. Both compute session keys and encrypt immediately.
lessonCards.example: Reduces connection latency from 2-RTT to 1-RTT (and supports 0-RTT resumption).

lessonCards.title: HTTPS: The Padlock of the Web
lessonCards.analogy: Wrapping standard HTTP web traffic in an unbreakable TLS encryption envelope.
lessonCards.coreConcept: HTTPS (port 443) runs HTTP over TLS. It guarantees Confidentiality (preventing ISPs and coffee shops from sniffing passwords) and Authenticity (proving you connected to your real bank).
lessonCards.example: Modern browsers flag plain unencrypted HTTP sites as 'Not Secure'.

lessonCards.title: Wireless Security: WPA2 vs WPA3
lessonCards.analogy: WPA2 checked passwords like a loud shouted whisper; WPA3 Dragonfly handshake checks passwords without leaking them.
lessonCards.coreConcept: WPA2 used a 4-way handshake vulnerable to offline dictionary cracking (KRACK attack). WPA3 uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), defeating offline password cracking even on weak passphrases.
lessonCards.example: WPA3 also enforces Protected Management Frames (PMF) to prevent Wi-Fi deauthentication attacks.

questions.prompt: How many round-trip times (RTT) does a full handshake take in modern TLS 1.3 compared to legacy TLS 1.2?
options: TLS 1.3 takes 1-RTT (50% faster than TLS 1.2's 2-RTT)
TLS 1.3 takes 10-RTT
Both take 5-RTT
TLS 1.3 takes zero seconds
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 sends the client's Diffie-Hellman key share speculatively in the very first ClientHello packet, completing key exchange in a single round trip.
wrongExplanations: Correct! 1-RTT handshake dramatically speeds up web page load times.
10-RTT would make web browsing intolerably slow.
Legacy TLS 1.2 required 2-RTT.
Handshakes take physical network transit time.
questions.realWorldExample: RFC 8446 standardized TLS 1.3 in 2018, deprecating RSA key exchange and broken CBC ciphers.

questions.prompt: Which ancient cryptographic feature was completely REMOVED from TLS 1.3 to guarantee Forward Secrecy?
options: Static RSA key exchange
Diffie-Hellman key exchange
AES encryption
SHA-256 hashing
questions.explanation: In TLS 1.3, RSA key exchange was completely abolished; all key exchanges MUST use Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) to guarantee forward secrecy.
wrongExplanations: Correct! RSA key exchange allowed anyone holding the server's private key to decrypt all past recorded traffic.
Diffie-Hellman is mandatory in TLS 1.3.
AES-GCM is standard.
SHA-256 is the default hash.
questions.realWorldExample: Removing static RSA prevents government surveillance agencies from storing encrypted traffic to decrypt years later.

questions.prompt: What vulnerability allowed attackers to capture WPA2 Wi-Fi handshakes and crack home passwords offline?
options: WPA2's 4-way handshake exposed cryptographic hashes derived directly from the pre-shared key (PSK)
Wi-Fi routers do not use radio waves
WPA2 keys only have 4 letters
Wi-Fi passwords expire every hour
questions.explanation: Attackers capture the 4-way EAPOL handshake frames over the air and run dictionary attacks on their GPU clusters at billions of guesses per second.
wrongExplanations: Correct! EAPOL frames leak the verification hash for offline brute-forcing without touching the router.
Wi-Fi transmits via 2.4GHz and 5GHz radio.
PSK passwords can be up to 63 characters.
Passphrases stay valid until changed.
questions.realWorldExample: Tools like Aircrack-ng and Hashcat routinely crack captured WPA2 handshakes.

questions.prompt: How does WPA3's Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE, 'Dragonfly') protocol defeat offline dictionary attacks?
options: It uses zero-knowledge password proofs: an attacker cannot verify a guessed password without active interactive router participation
It forces all passwords to be 100 characters
It disables radio signals
It requires smart cards for home routers
questions.explanation: SAE executes an interactive zero-knowledge exchange; a captured passive handshake provides zero mathematical proof of whether a password guess is correct.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Attackers cannot test password guesses offline against captured packets.
WPA3 supports standard user-chosen passphrases.
Radio signals are untouched.
Home WPA3 Personal requires no smart cards.
questions.realWorldExample: WPA3 dragonfly handshake is based on RFC 7664.

questions.prompt: What is HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)?
options: A security header that instructs browsers to ONLY connect via HTTPS, preventing SSL stripping attacks
A firewall that blocks games
A protocol that speeds up downloads
A tool to compress JPEG images
questions.explanation: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security header) forces browsers to automatically convert http:// to https:// before sending any network packets.
wrongExplanations: Correct! HSTS stops SSL-Strip attacks where adversaries downgrade connections to plain HTTP.
HSTS is a browser policy header, not a firewall.
HSTS enforces encryption, not download acceleration.
Compression is unrelated.
questions.realWorldExample: Major domains are included in browser 'HSTS Preload lists', ensuring connections are encrypted from the very first visit.

options: An attacker sends spoofed management frames commanding the victim's device to disconnect from the access point
An attacker cuts the router's physical power cord
An attacker jams the entire 5GHz frequency band
An attacker changes the router's brand name
questions.explanation: Because management frames were unencrypted in legacy Wi-Fi (802.11), attackers spoof disconnect packets to kick users off or force handshakes.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Spoofed deauth frames disconnect victims from Wi-Fi networks.
Physical sabotage is vandalism, not a protocol exploit.
Frequency jamming requires radio noise transmitters.
SSID broadcasting is separate.
questions.realWorldExample: WPA3 mandates Protected Management Frames (802.11w PMF) to cryptographically sign deauth packets.

ashRecap: TLS 1.3 gives the web a lightning-fast 1-round handshake with forward secrecy. WPA3 shields your Wi-Fi from eavesdroppers and offline password crackers!
